data.title: Multi-Factor Authentication Not Enforced for Privileged Access
data.summary: Administrative and remote access could be obtained with a password alone, so any credential that is phished, reused or guessed grants access directly. MFA is the single control that most reduces the value of stolen credentials.
data.description:
Credential theft is the dominant initial access vector, and password-only authentication makes every stolen credential immediately usable. Where MFA is absent from administrative interfaces, remote access or cloud consoles, phishing succeeds outright.

Partial deployment is the common state: MFA on the VPN but not on the cloud console, on email but not on the legacy application, or with exemptions for service accounts and break-glass accounts that are then used routinely.

The factor matters as well. Push approvals are vulnerable to fatigue attacks, and SMS and voice codes to interception and SIM swapping; phishing-resistant factors bound to the origin defeat the proxy-based kits now in general use.
data.recommendation:
* Require MFA for all administrative access, remote access and cloud consoles, with no standing exemptions.
* Prefer phishing-resistant factors — FIDO2 security keys or platform authenticators — for privileged accounts.
* Replace push approval with number matching where keys are not yet deployed.
* Protect break-glass accounts with hardware factors and monitor every use.
* Enforce MFA by conditional access policy rather than per-application configuration.
data.short_recommendation: Enforce phishing-resistant MFA on all privileged access.
